question: Sending finished work from this repo up to the shared server is something I was told you approved as a standing rule for every lane. That reached me through another session rather than from you, so I have treated it as unconfirmed and sent nothing on it. Nothing of mine is stuck behind it tonight, because everything here has already been sent. It matters for the next piece of work I finish, and two other lanes are holding finished work right now for the same reason.

options.name: Confirm it as standing permission
options.what: Each lane sends up its own finished work whenever it is ready, without asking again. I stop raising this and so do the other two lanes.
options.costs: Work leaves this machine as soon as it is finished, so a mistake becomes visible to everyone before you have seen it. Nothing becomes unfixable: a correction is sent on top the same way.

options.name: Keep asking every time
options.what: I ask you before each send, and so does every other lane.

question: The tools in this suite reach an emulator over a shared connection. There are two emulators: the old one, and the new one I have been building. Three lanes including this one have written down that they are waiting for you to change a setting so the tools reach the new one. I now think that is the wrong person. The thing that decides which emulator answers is whichever one was started first on that connection, not any setting, and starting it is something I can do from here. I want to confirm that by measuring it, and I want your word before I start a shared emulator that every other lane's tools would then be talking to.

options.name: Check it, and start the new emulator if I am right
options.what: I confirm which emulator is answering today, then start the new one on the shared connection. Every lane's tools begin reaching it, and the two lanes waiting on you stop waiting. Anything the new emulator cannot do yet refuses by name rather than returning a wrong answer, which is how we learn what to build next.
options.costs: About twenty minutes of my time. Stopping the program puts everything back exactly as it was. Other lanes may see some tools refuse by name for a few days while I build the missing pieces, which is the outcome you already said you wanted.

options.name: Check it and report back before starting anything
options.what: I confirm who actually has to perform the switch, write it down for the other lanes, and stop there.
options.costs: About twenty minutes, and then two lanes stay blocked until you have read the answer and ruled a second time.

options.name: You perform the switch yourself, as originally planned
options.what: You change the setting and relaunch the sessions, and I stay out of it.
options.costs: Your evening, and it may accomplish nothing, because I do not believe that setting is what decides which emulator answers.

recommend.because: You already ruled that we should switch now and build the missing pieces as we run into them. This is that same ruling arriving at a step nobody had realised was mine to take. It is undone by stopping one program, and it frees two lanes tonight rather than after another round trip through you.

question: Your on-screen game window is not private: two lane sessions' debugging tools are wired straight into it, and it has been running one of aeon's work-in-progress builds rather than the one you launched since about 18:20 UTC today. Every suite session has the same wiring and would hit it on its first emulator command. How do you want it handled?

options.name: Relaunch the six lane sessions
options.what: Close and relaunch the lanes from the console. Each session's tooling reloads from disk on start, which is where the already-merged fix lives, so every lane goes back to opening its own private emulator.
options.costs: A few minutes of your time and six sessions restarted. Nothing is lost — every lane's state is written to its own files and the lanes are at or near clean stopping points. Your game window is untouched by this and keeps running.

options.name: Leave it; every lane just avoids the emulator
options.what: Nobody restarts anything. Each lane treats the emulator tools as unavailable for the rest of its life.
options.costs: It relies on six sessions all remembering, indefinitely. One forgotten command pauses, steps or writes into your game while you are playing it — which is exactly what already happened once today, in good faith.

options.what: Restart oracle and aeon; leave the other four, which have no emulator work in front of them.
options.costs: Cheaper now, and it leaves four sessions still wired to your window against the day one of them needs a quick emulator check.

recommend.because: The fix already exists and is merged; the only thing standing between you and it is that these processes started forty minutes before it landed. Restarting is the whole remedy, it costs nothing but minutes, and the alternative asks six sessions to remember a rule forever.

question: Breakpoints shipped last night with one gap I told you about: a breakpoint does not fire while your player window is running the game freely. I sent an agent to work out how the emulator should honestly SAY that, and the answer came back that there is nothing honest to say — the gap is total. While you are actually playing, a breakpoint cannot fire by any route at all. Do I close it, or leave it and just write it down?

options.name: Close it — make breakpoints work in your player window (Recommended)
options.what: Your game window pauses itself when a breakpoint hits, the same way it does when you pause it by hand, and the emulator announces the stop to any tool that is watching. Breakpoints then work everywhere, including in the window you actually use. The two pieces I thought were missing already exist; the real work is one ordering problem and making sure the stop is stamped with the right frame number instead of zero.
options.costs: A parcel that touches your player, not just the bus — so your window's behaviour changes: it will stop on its own when something arms a breakpoint. Half a day at most, and it holds the test lane while it runs. I would rather do this than publish a sentence saying the debugger does not work while you debug.

options.name: Leave it and declare the limitation in the emulator's own handshake
options.what: Every tool that connects is told up front that breakpoints do not fire in this arrangement, so nothing is surprised. Cheaper, and it is a legitimate thing to declare — the contract already lets an instrument state its own scope.
options.costs: You would be shipping a formal declaration that the feature does not work in the arrangement you personally use. It also needs a rules change agreed with the hub first, so it is not actually the fast option, and at the end of it the feature still does not work.

options.name: Write it in our notes and move on
options.what: Costs nothing today and keeps me on the remaining ten missing commands.
options.costs: A tool that hits this gets a wait that times out after a minute with nothing wrong on its face. One of aeon's tools is already pointed at exactly this and is saved today only by an unrelated spelling mismatch that they intend to fix. It would land on them, not on us.

because: What we would otherwise be declaring is that the debugger's main feature does not work in the window you use it in. I checked the cost myself rather than trusting the note that deferred it, and the note was wrong on both halves — the two mechanisms it said were missing are both already in the code, and the code's own comment said so while the note said otherwise. So this is a bounded fix that was deferred on an estimate that does not survive reading the source.

question: You asked for a file dialog and drag-and-drop. The dialog is built and works. Drag-and-drop turns out not to be a setting we switch on: the window toolkit we use has no file-drop support at all, and your desktop is Wayland, which is the harder of the two ways to add it by hand. How much do you want me to spend on it?

options.name: Skip the dragging, let you paste a path instead (Recommended)
options.what: The ROM picker already has a line you type into to filter the list. If what you type looks like a path, it offers that file directly — so you can copy a path from anywhere and open it, which is what most people are reaching for drag-and-drop to do. Works the same whichever desktop you are on.
options.costs: About twenty lines and an hour. You still cannot literally drag a file onto the window.

options.name: Build real drag-and-drop for your desktop
options.what: You drag a ROM from your file manager onto the game window and it loads.
options.costs: A parcel of its own, and the delicate kind: our window library does not model drops, so I would be attaching our own handler onto the connection it already owns, with a new dependency. Roughly a day, and the failure mode if I get it wrong is your window hanging rather than a wrong answer on screen.

options.name: Build it the easy way, which does not work on your desktop as launched
options.what: Drag-and-drop under X11. We already have the pieces for that one.
options.costs: Half a day, and you would have to start the player with --x11 every time for it to do anything. I do not recommend paying for a feature that is off by default on your own machine.

options.name: The picker is enough
options.what: Nothing more is built. Press O, pick a game.
options.costs: Nothing. If you find yourself wanting to drag files later, this card is still here.

recommend.because: It gets you the thing dragging is for — opening a ROM you already have the location of, without relaunching — for an hour instead of a day, and it works on both desktops rather than only one. Real drag-and-drop is worth building if you actually want to drag; it is not worth building to save a paste.

detail: MEASURED, not assumed. minifb 0.28 has no file-drop support of any kind (grepped its lib.rs: the only drag/drop matches are `target_os = "dragonfly"` and a cursor-shape doc comment). The owner's session is XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland / WAYLAND_DISPLAY=wayland-0, and his running player (pid 3614020) carries no --x11, so his window is a native Wayland surface, not XWayland. minifb DOES expose WaylandWindowHandle and WaylandDisplayHandle (wayland.rs:1260-1286), so the Wayland option is possible rather than blocked -- it means binding our own registry/seat/wl_data_device on minifb's own wl_display with our own event queue, plus a wayland-client dependency. The X11 route would be hand-rolled XDND, for which icon.rs is the in-tree precedent (it already reaches minifb's raw handle and calls XSetClassHint) and x11-dl is already a direct dependency. Full reasoning and the firsthand greps: docs/2026-08-28-rom-open.md section 4. The picker half is landed independently and depends on none of this.

question: The sound is dull and I think I know why: your player turns on a filter by default that imitates a real Mega Drive's audio output stage, and it rolls off everything above about 3.4 kHz. The emulator core does not do this — only the player does. Turning it off is not a bug fix, it is a taste decision, and your own standing rule says accuracy-matching stays and taste deviations do not. So it is yours. Listen once each way before you answer: put ORACLE_CONSOLE_FILTER=off in front of the player command for none at all, or =va3 for a darker console.

options.name: Keep the filter on — stay accuracy-pure
options.what: The player keeps imitating the console's real output stage, and the dullness is what the hardware actually sounded like.
options.costs: The sound stays as it is. If it is bothering you every time you play, that cost is real and recurring.

options.name: Default it off — brighter, less faithful
options.what: The player stops filtering by default. You get the full brightness the chips produce.
options.costs: We would be shipping a deliberate deviation from the hardware as the default, which is the thing your standing rule bars. I would want it recorded as a taste choice rather than quietly done, and the accurate mode kept available.

options.name: Leave the default alone, let the player remember YOUR choice
options.what: Default stays accurate for anyone else; your setting persists between runs the way volume already does, so you set it once.
options.costs: A small amount of work. It also means you and a fresh install hear different things, so a future 'the sound changed' is harder to diagnose.

recommend.because: It gets you the sound you want without making the emulator ship a deliberate inaccuracy as its default, which is the line your own rule draws. It is also the only option that does not need you to be sure — you can change it any evening. I would rather not pick between the first two on your behalf: which one is right depends on what you want this to BE, and that is not a measurement I can take.

question: I split my notes file today: everything finished moved to a second file nobody reads at startup, and it went from 298 KB to 153 KB with nothing lost. The suite limit is 100 KB, so it is still over by about a third. What is left is not history - it is 37 KB of hard-won house rules, 26 KB of operating lessons and the live work list, each rule wrapped in the story of the mistake that earned it. The suite's own rule says trimming those is your call and not mine, so I stopped rather than cut. How do you want the rest handled?

options.name: Let me shorten the stories but keep every rule word-for-word (Recommended)
options.what: Each rule stays exactly as written; the tale of the mistake behind it moves to the finished-history file, one search away. Nothing is deleted and it is reversible. Should land close to the limit.
options.costs: A rule is easier to talk yourself out of when the story of what it cost is not sitting underneath it. My own file says in as many words: do not thin these. So there is a real risk a future session reads a bare rule and does not feel the weight of it.

options.name: Leave it at 153 KB and let me report the overage
options.what: Nothing is touched. Every rule keeps its story. I stay over the limit and say so.
options.costs: Every session I start pays about half again what the limit intends, and that is a cost you pay all day across six lanes. The rule stays broken on purpose, which invites the next person to ignore it too.

question: I split my notes file today: everything finished moved to a second file nobody reads at startup, and it went from 298 KB to 153 KB with nothing lost. The suite limit is 100 KB, so it is still over by about a third. What is left is not history - it is 37 KB of hard-won house rules, 26 KB of operating lessons and the live work list, each rule wrapped in the story of the mistake that earned it. The suite's own rule says trimming those is your call and not mine, so I stopped rather than cut. How do you want the rest handled?

options.what: Each rule stays exactly as written; the tale of the mistake behind it moves to the finished-history file, one search away. Nothing is deleted and it is reversible. Should land close to the limit.
options.costs: A rule is easier to talk yourself out of when the story of what it cost is not sitting underneath it. My own file says in as many words: do not thin these. So there is a real risk a future session reads a bare rule and does not feel the weight of it.

options.costs: Every session I start pays about half again what the limit intends, and that is a cost you pay all day across six lanes. The rule stays broken on purpose, which invites the next person to ignore it too.

question: You said not everything works as a lens and you want oracle-old's window back - tabs, and dragging debug panels to whichever side you want. I can do that, but the shape is a look call and it is yours. The player draws its own window on a bare framebuffer: there is no toolkit underneath it, so tabs, dragging, panel edges and remembering your layout are all things I write by hand. That is why the three options below differ so much in size rather than in polish.

options.name: Panels that dock to a side you choose, with tabs (Recommended)
options.what: Left, right and bottom docks. Any debug panel can be dragged onto a dock and lands there as a tab; drag it to another side and it moves. Widths draggable, and your layout is remembered between runs. The four debug views you have now become panels.
options.costs: You cannot split a side into two stacked panels or nest them like a full workspace - each side is one tab strip. If what you liked about oracle-old was arranging panels freely rather than just choosing a side, this will feel short of it and I would be rebuilding toward the next option later.

options.name: The full oracle-old model - drag anywhere, split, nest
options.what: A real docking workspace: drop a panel against any edge of any existing panel and the space splits, nests to any depth, tabs everywhere, layouts saved and switchable.
options.costs: Several sessions rather than one, and every piece of it is written from scratch on a bare framebuffer - the drop zones, the split tree, the resize handles, the keyboard focus. It is the thing you described, and it is the most expensive way to find out whether you wanted the simpler version.

options.name: Rebuild the window on a real UI toolkit first
options.what: Move the player onto an off-the-shelf immediate-mode toolkit, where docking, tabs and layout persistence largely already exist, and draw the game picture into it. Future debug UI gets much cheaper.
options.costs: It replaces the window wholesale, so everything you already recognise - the status line, toasts, the ROM picker, the lenses, the font - gets rebuilt and will not look identical. That is a big change to the thing you use every day, made for future convenience rather than for anything you asked for.

recommend.because: It is the option that actually matches the sentence you wrote - tabs, and dragging a panel to another side - without me building a whole workspace engine to find out. You would have it in useful shape soonest, and if it turns out you want free arrangement after living with it, the panels and tabs built here are the same pieces the fuller version needs.

detail: Owner ask relayed by the hub, his words verified at empyrean c92e036. Not started; no build until he picks (per the ask). Sizing grounded firsthand: crates/oracle-frontend is minifb 0.28 (raw framebuffer, no toolkit) at 16,060 lines over 24 hand-rolled modules incl. its own font.rs, overlay.rs, palette.rs picker and four lens/ modules. Board row DEBUG-PANELS, size L. Lenses stay for what they suit.
